*Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then*

$$
\iiint\limits_R \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} \: \textrm{d}V
=
\iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{n}\:\mathrm{d}S
$$

*where $\mathbf{n}$ is the outward-pointing unit normal to $S.$*

In other words, the sum of the microscopic "fluxes" (divergences) of $\mathbf{F}$ inside $R$ equals the macroscopic flux of $\mathbf{F}$ through the boundary of $R.$ 

The divergence theorem can be summarized in a single diagram.

![](images/ff/ffabcceb5f4fd520a57f909c476b267f584ac4dc3fb948a5c1996b71dbc74e6f.png)

$$

![](images/cf/cf90197ac99a066db75154200de4cbee2494fef15deed6be7b7c4cd501ae8f26.png)

 

Let's find the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

To find the total flux directly, we would need to find the flux through each of the six surfaces of our rectangular solid and then add the results. However, using the divergence theorem

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}
= \iiint\limits_R \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} \: \textrm{d}V,
$$

we can reduce this computation to a single triple integral.

Computing the divergence of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+1)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3z)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy) \\  & =2+0+0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}

$$

$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134012 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

*Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then*

$$
\iiint\limits_R \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} \: \textrm{d}V
=
\iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{n}\:\mathrm{d}S
$$

= \iiint\limits_R \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} \: \textrm{d}V,
$$

we can reduce this computation to a single triple integral.

Computing the divergence of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+1)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3z)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy) \\  & =2+0+0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux through $S$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}2\,\text{d}V \\  & =2{∭}_{R}\,\text{d}V \\  & =2\cdot \text{Volume}(R) \\  & =2\cdot (3\cdot 2\cdot 1) \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e318cc2d-81e3-5cbd-b0ce-2f076bfd06b8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7732 :tutorial/title "Calculating the Flux Across a Surface"} {:db/id 17592186135170 :tutorial/content "The **divergence theorem** is a higher-dimensional analog of Green's theorem in flux form. It states the following:

> *Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then*
> 
> 
> $$
> \iiint\limits_R \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} \: \textrm{d}V
> =
> \iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}
> =
> \iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{n}\:\mathrm{d}S
> $$
> 
> 
> *where $\mathbf{n}$ is the outward-pointing unit normal to $S.$*

In other words, the sum of the microscopic "fluxes" (divergences) of $\mathbf{F}$ inside $R$ equals the macroscopic flux of $\mathbf{F}$ through the boundary of $R.$
